E0101.text:
The parser met a token it can't use at that point: a missing `then`, `do`,
`end` or closing parenthesis, a stray operator, or `...` outside a vararg
function. The message names what was expected and the token found instead
("near '<eof>'" means the file ended too early). WoW would refuse to load the
file with the same Lua syntax error, so it is an error in every file.

The same code is reported for wowlua syntax (a type annotation, `+=`, `?.`,
…) in a `.lua` file, which stays plain Lua 5.1: rename the file to `.wowlua`,
or write the code in Lua.

files.text:
local hp = UnitHealth("player")
if hp > 0
    print(hp)
end

examples.output:
error[E0101]: 'then' expected near 'print'
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:3:5
  │
3 │     print(hp)
  │     ^^^^^ here

files.text:
local hp = UnitHealth("player")
if hp > 0 then
    print(hp)
end

E0102.text:
A string runs to the end of its line, or a long string or long comment
(`[[ … ]]`, `--[==[ … ]==]`) or a backtick string runs to the end of the
file, without its closing delimiter. Quoted strings (`"…"`, `'…'`) cannot span
lines, as in Lua 5.1: close the string on the same line, or use a long string
or a backtick string for text with line breaks.

files.text:
local greeting = "Welcome back
print(greeting)

examples.output:
error[E0102]: unfinished string
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:1:18
  │
1 │ local greeting = "Welcome back
  │                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ here

files.text:
local greeting = "Welcome back"
print(greeting)

E0103.text:
A number literal is malformed, such as `1e`, `3..2` or `0xG`, or uses a `_`
digit separator in the wrong place. wowlua allows `_` between two digits of
the same run (`1_000_000`, `0xFF_FF`, `3.141_592`, `0b1010_1010`), but not at
the start or end, twice in a row, or next to `.`, `e`, `x`, `b` or a sign:
`1__0`, `_1`, `1_`, `1_.5`, `0x_FF` and `1e_5` are all E0103.

files.text:
local maxGold = 1__000_000
print(maxGold)

examples.output:
error[E0103]: malformed number (misplaced `_` digit separator) near '1__000_000'
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:1:17
  │
1 │ local maxGold = 1__000_000
  │                 ^^^^^^^^^^ here

files.text:
local maxGold = 1_000_000
print(maxGold)

E0104.text:
A line starts with `(` right after an expression that could be called, so it
reads as a call that spans two lines. Lua 5.1 rejects this as "ambiguous
syntax (function call x new statement)", and wowlua does too. If you meant a
call, put the `(` on the same line as the function. If you meant a new
statement, start it differently (assign the parenthesized value to a local).

files.text:
local show = print
show
("ready")

examples.output:
error[E0104]: ambiguous syntax (function call x new statement)
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:3:1
  │
3 │ ("ready")
  │ ^ here

files.text:
local show = print
show("ready")

E0105.text:
A backtick string contains an escape it doesn't know. Backtick strings take
Lua's escapes (`\n`, `\t`, `\\`, `\"`, `\ddd`, …) plus `\{`, `\}`, `` \` ``,
`\xXX` (two hex digits), `\u{XXXX}` and `\z`; anything else, such as `\q` or
the `\A` of a WoW path, is an error. Quoted strings keep Lua 5.1's rule, where
an unknown escape yields the character itself, so the same text may work in
`"…"` and fail in a backtick string. Write `\\` for a backslash.

files.text:
local name = "MyAddon"
print(`{name} lives in Interface\AddOns`)

examples.output:
error[E0105]: invalid escape `\A` in a backtick string
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:2:33
  │
2 │ print(`{name} lives in Interface\AddOns`)
  │                                 ^^ here

files.text:
local name = "MyAddon"
print(`{name} lives in Interface\\AddOns`)

E0106.text:
A `break` or `continue` is not inside a loop of the same function. Both only
leave or restart the innermost `while`, `repeat` or `for` loop; a loop around
the function that contains them doesn't count. Use `return` to leave a
function early.

files.text:
local function onEvent(event: string)
    if event ~= "PLAYER_LOGIN" then
        break
    end
    print("logged in")
end
onEvent("PLAYER_LOGIN")

examples.output:
error[E0106]: no loop to break near 'end'
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:3:9
  │
3 │         break
  │         ^^^^^ here

files.text:
local function onEvent(event: string)
    if event ~= "PLAYER_LOGIN" then
        return
    end
    print("logged in")
end
onEvent("PLAYER_LOGIN")

E0107.text:
`continue` is used in a `repeat … until cond` loop whose condition reads a
local declared in the loop body. Lua 5.1 has no `goto`, so wowlua wraps the
body in an inner loop to implement `continue`, and the body's locals would no
longer be visible to `until`. Declare the local before the loop and assign it
in the body, or use another kind of loop.

files.text:
local i = 0
repeat
    i += 1
    local finished = i >= 10
    if i % 2 == 0 then continue end
    print(i)
until finished

examples.output:
error[E0107]: `continue` cannot be used in this `repeat` loop: its `until` condition uses the body local `finished`
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:7:7
  │
7 │ until finished
  │       ^^^^^^^^ here

files.text:
local i = 0
local finished = false
repeat
    i += 1
    finished = i >= 10
    if i % 2 == 0 then continue end
    print(i)
until finished

E0108.text:
`import` or `export` is inside a block (a function, `if`, loop or `do`).
Both only work at the top level of a file: imports are resolved when the
file loads, and exports become the module's table. Move the `import` to the
top of the file, and export a top-level declaration.

files.text:
local function start()
    import after from "wowlua:timer"
    after(1, function() print("started") end)
end
start()

examples.output:
error[E0108]: `import` is only allowed at the top level of a file
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:2:5
  │
2 │     import after from "wowlua:timer"
  │     ^^^^^^ here

files.text:
import after from "wowlua:timer"

local function start()
    after(1, function() print("started") end)
end
start()

E0109.text:
A decorator (`@name` or `@name(…)`) stands before a statement that can't be
decorated, such as a call or an assignment. Decorators apply to declarations:
functions, `local`, `const`, classes, class members, enums and the like. Put
the decorator right before the declaration it is meant for.

files.text:
@deprecated
print("old API")

examples.output:
error[E0109]: a decorator must be followed by a declaration (function, local, const, class, …)
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:1:1
  │  
1 │ ╭ @deprecated
2 │ │ print("old API")
  │ ╰────────────────^ here

files.text:
@deprecated
local function oldApi()
    print("old API")
end

E0110.text:
`??` is mixed with `and` or `or` in one expression without parentheses, as
in `a ?? b or c`. They have the same precedence, and the reading isn't
obvious (`??` keeps `false`, `or` doesn't), so wowlua asks for parentheses, as
JavaScript does. Add them around the part that should go first.

files.text:
local saved: boolean? = nil
local fallback = true
print(saved ?? fallback or false)

examples.output:
error[E0110]: `??` cannot be mixed with `and`/`or` without parentheses
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:3:25
  │
3 │ print(saved ?? fallback or false)
  │                         ^^ here

files.text:
local saved: boolean? = nil
local fallback = true
print((saved ?? fallback) or false)

E0111.text:
A compound assignment (`+=`, `..=`, `??=`, …) has several targets, as in
`a, b += 1`. Compound assignment takes exactly one target; write one
statement per variable.

files.text:
local kills, deaths = 0, 0
kills, deaths += 1
print(kills, deaths)

examples.output:
error[E0111]: compound assignment has a single target
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:2:15
  │
2 │ kills, deaths += 1
  │               ^^ here

files.text:
local kills, deaths = 0, 0
kills += 1
deaths += 1
print(kills, deaths)

E0112.text:
A `const` has no `= value`, or declares several names (`const A, B = 1, 2`).
A constant can't be assigned later, so it needs its value where it is
declared, and each `const` declares one name. Use one `const` per value, or
`local` for a value that is set later.

files.text:
const MAX_ITEMS
print(MAX_ITEMS)

examples.output:
error[E0112]: `const` needs an initializer
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:1:1
  │
1 │ const MAX_ITEMS
  │ ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ here

files.text:
const MAX_ITEMS = 40
print(MAX_ITEMS)

E0113.text:
An optional chain (`?.`, `?.[`, `?:`) is the target of an assignment or a
compound assignment, as in `t.inner?.n = 1`. If the chain stopped at `nil`
there would be nothing to assign to. Test the value first and assign
through a plain access.

files.text:
local settings: { frame: { scale: number }? } = {}
settings.frame?.scale = 1

examples.output:
error[E0113]: an optional chain cannot be assigned to
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:2:1
  │
2 │ settings.frame?.scale = 1
  │ ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ here

files.text:
local settings: { frame: { scale: number }? } = {}
if settings.frame then
    settings.frame.scale = 1
end

E0114.text:
`continue` is followed by more statements in its block. Like `break` and
`return`, it must be the last statement of its block, because the code after
it could never run. Write `do continue end` to continue from the middle of a
block, or put it inside an `if`.

files.text:
for i = 1, 3 do
    continue
    print(i)
end

examples.output:
error[E0114]: `continue` must be the last statement of its block; write `do continue end`
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:3:5
  │
3 │     print(i)
  │     ^^^^^ here

files.text:
for i = 1, 3 do
    if i == 2 then continue end
    print(i)
end

E0115.text:
A `class`, `abstract class`, `enum`, `declare` or `overload function` stands
inside a block (a function, `if`, loop or `do`). They may only appear at the
top level of a file: each class and enum is exactly one runtime table, and
declarations and overloads describe the file's top-level names. Move the
declaration to the top level. (`type` and `interface` may appear in any
block.)

files.text:
local function setup()
    enum Mode { Simple, Advanced }
    return Mode.Simple
end
print(setup())

examples.output:
error[E0115]: `enum` is only allowed at the top level of a file
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:2:5
  │
2 │     enum Mode { Simple, Advanced }
  │     ^^^^ here

files.text:
enum Mode { Simple, Advanced }

local function setup()
    return Mode.Simple
end
print(setup())

E0116.text:
A backtick string contains a `}` that doesn't close an embedded `{…}`
expression. Write `\}` for a literal closing brace (and `\{` for an opening
one).

files.text:
local count = 3
print(`count} items: {count}`)

examples.output:
error[E0116]: unbalanced `}` in an interpolated string; write `\}` for a literal brace
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:2:13
  │
2 │ print(`count} items: {count}`)
  │             ^ here

files.text:
local count = 3
print(`\{count\} items: {count}`)

E0117.text:
`import _` is combined with other names, as in `import _, clamp from "./math"`.
`import _` only makes sure a file loads first and binds nothing, so it must be
the only name in its import. A named import already loads its module first,
so drop the `_`.

files.text:
import _, clamp from "./math"
print(clamp(5, 0, 1))

examples.output:
error[E0117]: `import _` cannot be combined with other names
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:1:8
  │
1 │ import _, clamp from "./math"
  │        ^ here

files.text:
import clamp from "./math"
print(clamp(5, 0, 1))

E0118.text:
`export function` is followed by a dotted or method name (`M.f`, `M:m`).
An export names a module-level local, so it takes a plain name. Export the
function by its own name, or export the table and add functions to it.

examples.output:
error[E0118]: `export function` takes a plain name
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:2:17
  │
2 │ export function M.greet()
  │                 ^^^^^^^ here

E0119.text:
An `export local` has no initializer. Exported bindings can't be assigned
after their declaration (E1010), so the value must be given where it is
exported. For state that changes, export a table and change its contents.

files.text: export local count: number

examples.output:
error[E0119]: `export local` needs an initializer
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:1:1
  │
1 │ export local count: number
  │ ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ here

files.text: export local count: number = 0

E1001.text:
In strict mode, the code reads a global that nothing declares: no WoW API,
Lua library, `declare global`, SavedVariable from the manifest,
`check.globals` entry, or global that a file of the package assigns. Most
often it is a typo or a missing `local`; in game the read gives `nil` and
fails later with "attempt to call/index a nil value". Fix the name, make it
a local or an import, or declare the global (`declare global name: T`).

Strict mode comes from `--!strict` or the manifest (`check.mode`,
`check.strict`). In basic mode, the default, the same read is the warning
W1001. An existence test (`if SomeApi then … end`) never reports the tested
name.

files.text:
--!strict
local playerName = UnitName("player")
print(playerNmae)

examples.output:
error[E1001]: `playerNmae` is not a declared global
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:3:7
  │
3 │ print(playerNmae)
  │       ^^^^^^^^^^ here

files.text:
--!strict
local playerName = UnitName("player")
print(playerName)

W1001.text:
The code reads a global that nothing declares (see E1001 for what counts as
declared). It is a warning in basic mode, the default, and in plain Lua
files; strict mode makes it the error E1001. Usually it is a typo or a
missing `local`, and the value is `nil` in game. Fix the name, or declare a
global that comes from somewhere the checker can't see: `declare global`, or
the manifest's `check.globals` for another addon's globals.

files.text:
local playerName = UnitName("player")
print(playerNmae)

examples.output:
warning[W1001]: `playerNmae` is not a declared global
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:2:7
  │
2 │ print(playerNmae)
  │       ^^^^^^^^^^ here

files.text:
local playerName = UnitName("player")
print(playerName)

E1002.text:
In strict mode, the code assigns a global that isn't declared, including
through `function name()` in a script. Accidental globals are a classic addon
bug: they leak into every addon's environment, can collide with other addons'
names and can taint Blizzard code. Make it `local` if only this file needs
it, export it from a module, or declare a real global (`declare global
name: T`). Writing `_G.name = value` is always allowed.

In basic mode the same assignment is the warning W1002.

files.text:
--!strict
counter = 0

examples.output:
error[E1002]: assigns the undeclared global `counter` (declare it, use `_G.counter`, or make it `local`)
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:2:1
  │
2 │ counter = 0
  │ ^^^^^^^ here

files.text:
--!strict
declare global MyAddonCounter: number
MyAddonCounter = 0

W1002.text:
The code assigns a global that isn't declared (see E1002). It is a warning in
basic mode, the default, and in plain Lua files; strict mode makes it the
error E1002. If the global is meant to exist (a SavedVariable, an API for
other addons), declare it or write `_G.name = value`; otherwise make it
`local`.

files.text: counter = 0

examples.output:
warning[W1002]: assigns the undeclared global `counter` (declare it, use `_G.counter`, or make it `local`)
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:1:1
  │
1 │ counter = 0
  │ ^^^^^^^ here

files.text:
local counter = 0
print(counter)

E1003.text:
A name used in a wowlua construct, such as a decorator argument, is not a
local or upvalue in scope there, nor a declared global. A decorator's
arguments are evaluated where the declaration is, when the file loads, so
the name must exist there. It is an error in every mode, where reading an
undeclared global elsewhere is W1001 or E1001. Declare the local before the
declaration, or fix the name.

files.text:
import throttle from "wowlua:timer"

@throttle(delay)
local function refresh()
end
refresh()

examples.output:
error[E1003]: `delay` is not a local, an upvalue or a declared global here: decorator arguments are evaluated where the declaration is
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:3:11
  │
3 │ @throttle(delay)
  │           ^^^^^ here

files.text:
import throttle from "wowlua:timer"

local delay = 0.5

@throttle(delay)
local function refresh()
end
refresh()

W1003.text:
A local, parameter, loop variable or import is never read. It is often a
leftover of a refactoring, or a sign that the wrong name is used somewhere.
Remove it, or start its name with `_` (`_event`) to keep it on purpose, as
for a callback parameter you must accept but don't need. Like every lint, its
level can be changed in the manifest's `check.lints` (`"W1003": "allow"`).

files.text:
local function greet(name: string, title: string)
    print("Hello " .. name)
end
greet("Ana", "Dr.")

examples.output:
warning[W1003]: unused parameter `title`
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:1:36
  │
1 │ local function greet(name: string, title: string)
  │                                    ^^^^^ never read
  │
  = help: prefix it with `_` (`_title`)

files.text:
local function greet(name: string, _title: string)
    print("Hello " .. name)
end
greet("Ana", "Dr.")

E1004.text:
A parameter's default value reads that parameter or a later one. Every
parameter is in scope in a default, as in the Lua it compiles to, so the
name means the parameter itself, which isn't set yet: it is `nil` there,
even when an outer local has the same name. A default may read earlier
parameters only. Reorder the parameters, or rename the parameter to read an
outer local of that name.

files.text:
local function resize(width: number = height, height: number = 100)
    print(width, height)
end
resize()

examples.output:
error[E1004]: `height` here is the parameter, which is not set yet (a default reads only earlier parameters); to read an outer `height`, give the parameter another name
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:1:39
  │
1 │ local function resize(width: number = height, height: number = 100)
  │                                       ^^^^^^ here

files.text:
local function resize(height: number = 100, width: number = height)
    print(width, height)
end
resize()

W1004.text:
A local hides another one: it has the name of a local of an enclosing scope,
or a `local function` is named like a local declared before it in the same
block (from there on, the earlier one is out of reach, even inside the new
function). A parameter named `self` in a class's method or constructor also
gets this warning, because it hides the instance. Hidden names are a common
source of "it reads the wrong value" bugs; rename one of them. Names starting
with `_` are exempt.

files.text:
local count = 1
do
    local count = 2
    print(count)
end
print(count)

examples.output:
warning[W1004]: `count` shadows a local of an enclosing scope
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:3:11
  │
1 │ local count = 1
  │       ----- shadowed local
2 │ do
3 │     local count = 2
  │           ^^^^^ declared here

files.text:
local count = 1
do
    local bonus = 2
    print(bonus)
end
print(count)

W1005.text:
Code follows a statement that execution never gets past: a `do return end`
(or `break`, `continue`), an `if` whose every branch returns or breaks, or a
call that never returns, such as `error(…)`. The code after it can never run.
Remove it, or move it before the statement that leaves.

files.text:
local function sign(x: number): number
    if x >= 0 then return 1 else return -1 end
    print("never printed")
end
print(sign(2))

examples.output:
warning[W1005]: unreachable code
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:3:5
  │
3 │     print("never printed")
  │     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ here

files.text:
local function sign(x: number): number
    print("checking", x)
    if x >= 0 then return 1 else return -1 end
end
print(sign(2))

E1010.text:
The code assigns to an exported `local` after its declaration, or to an
imported name. Importers copy an export once while the file loads, so a
later assignment would never reach them; exported and imported bindings are
therefore read-only. Change a table's contents instead (`state.count += 1`),
or export functions that read and change the value.

files.text:
export local count = 0
count = count + 1

examples.output:
error[E1010]: cannot assign to the exported binding `count`; mutate a table's contents or export accessor functions
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:2:1
  │
2 │ count = count + 1
  │ ^^^^^ here

files.text:
export local state = { count = 0 }
state.count = state.count + 1

E1011.text:
A top-level `import` comes after another statement. Imports must come first
in a module, before any other statement (comments and `--!` directives may
precede them). Move every import to the top of the file.

files.text:
local delay = 1
import after from "wowlua:timer"
after(delay, function() print("later") end)

examples.output:
error[E1011]: imports must come before every other statement
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:2:1
  │
2 │ import after from "wowlua:timer"
  │ ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ this import follows other code

files.text:
import after from "wowlua:timer"
local delay = 1
after(delay, function() print("later") end)

E1012.text:
An import names something the module doesn't export: a typo, a name that
was renamed or removed, or a function the module defines without `export`.
Check the module's `export` declarations and fix the name, or export it
there.

files.text:
import sleepFor from "wowlua:timer"
sleepFor(1)

examples.output:
error[E1012]: module has no export named `sleepFor`
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:1:8
  │
1 │ import sleepFor from "wowlua:timer"
  │        ^^^^^^^^ not exported

files.text:
import after from "wowlua:timer"
after(1, function() print("later") end)

E1013.text:
An import's path differs in case from the file on disk (`"./Math"` for
`math.wowlua`). Module paths are case-sensitive everywhere: WoW on Windows
would tolerate the mismatch, other systems would not find the file. Write
the path exactly as the file is named.

files.text:
import clamp from "./Math"
print(clamp(5, 0, 1))

examples.output:
error[E1013]: `./Math` differs in case from the file `math.wowlua`
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:1:19
  │
1 │ import clamp from "./Math"
  │                   ^^^^^^^^ here

files.text:
import clamp from "./math"
print(clamp(5, 0, 1))

E1014.text:
Files depend on each other in a cycle, and at least one dependency is needed
while a file loads. WoW loads files one after another, so one of them would
run before the other has defined what it uses. Modules may import each other
as long as the uses only happen later (inside functions called from events,
timers or handlers); a top-level call is what makes a use load-time. The
message shows the cycle and the calls that lead to each load-time use. Move
the use into a function that runs later, or move the shared code into a
third module.

files.text:
import greet from "./other"
export function hello(): string
    return "hi"
end
print(greet())

import hello from "./main"
export function greet(): string
    return hello() .. "!"
end
print(greet())

examples.output:
error[E1014]: load-time dependency cycle between main.wowlua, other.wowlua
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:5:7
  │
5 │ print(greet())
  │       ^^^^^ `main.wowlua` uses the import `greet` from `other.wowlua` while it loads
  │
  ┌─ src/other.wowlua:3:12
  │
3 │     return hello() .. "!"
  │            ----- `other.wowlua` uses the import `hello` from `main.wowlua` while it loads
  │
  = note: main.wowlua: in top-level code
  = note: other.wowlua: in greet, called from top-level code
  = help: move the use into a function that runs later (an event handler, for example), or split a module

files.text:
import greet from "./other"
export function hello(): string
    return "hi"
end
print(greet())

import hello from "./main"
export function greet(): string
    return hello() .. "!"
end

E1015.text:
The module an import names can't be found: no file at that path (tried with
`.wowlua`, `.d.wowlua`, `.lua` and `/init.wowlua`), an unknown

`local`, function, `const`, class, enum or import), or a name is exported
twice. An export is itself a module-level local, so the two would shadow
each other. Rename one of them, or put `export` on the original declaration.

for different flavors may share a name.

(`_G["x" .. i]`, `ns[key]`), or names come from outside the package. Give the
name a single defining file, or fix the order with an import (`import _
from "./file"`) or `build.load-order`.

Two modules import each other (a cycle that only runs later, which is
allowed), and the one checked first reads an export of the other that has
no type annotation. The modules of a cycle are checked in source order, so
that export's type isn't known yet and reads as `any` there: mistakes in its
use go unnoticed. Annotate the export in its module (`export local items:
string[] = {}`). The same applies to a `typeof` type alias of the later
module, and to file-level locals read through `import internal` in tests.

  │        ^^^^^ read as `any`
  │

or `@if` is given more than one condition. Conditions may use `wowlua:meta`

not `const`s, because each flavor's import graph is built before constants
are evaluated. For a runtime decision, use an ordinary `if`.

are compiled into, so another addon's module isn't part of this one. Use

E2003.text:
The value has no field or method of that name. Classes are sealed, so every
member of a class instance must be declared in the class body, in every mode;
a misspelt name is the usual cause. Strict mode also reports a named field
read from an array, an unknown field in a table literal written for a record
type, and a name the `string` library doesn't have (`s:nope()`), all of which
Lua would read as `nil`.

The code has two more meanings. A method defined outside its class body
(`function Animal:speak() … end` after the class) is E2003: move it into the
class. And the key `__wowlua` is reserved for the wowlua runtime, so assigning
it on a frame or an instance is E2003 too.

than you think, or a field's name is wrong; narrow an `unknown` with

E2005.text:
Strict mode only: the value may be `nil`, and it is used where `nil` doesn't
fit, such as calling a method on it, indexing it or passing it for a
parameter that doesn't take `nil`. In game that is the "attempt to index a nil
value" error. Check the value first (`if s then … end`, `assert(s)`, or an
early `return`), give a default with `??` or `or`, or make the target
optional (`T?`).

Basic mode lets `nil` into every type, so this code only appears in files
under `--!strict` or `check.mode = "strict"`.

    return xs[1]
end
local s = first({ "a" })
print(s:upper())

  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:6:9
  │
6 │ print(s:upper())
  │         ^^^^^ here

extra ones silently, which usually hides a mistake: a wrong function, or
arguments in the wrong order. Remove the extra arguments, or add the
parameters (`...: T` for any number of them).

W2055 instead; strict mode reports E2006 for every function.

neither is assignable to the other, and they aren't both tables. An assertion

checker counts the values of the package's own functions whose every
`return` gives a fixed number of them (local functions, a module's functions,

`and` or `or` that ends a `local` or an assignment, since those give one
value: in `local x, y = pos and pos:GetXY()`, `y` is always `nil`. Fix the
names, or write `if pos then x, y = pos:GetXY() end`. Names starting with

(`"check": { "lints": { "W2063": "warn" } }`). Names starting with `_` are

code is also reported when a class without a superclass calls `super(...)`,
and when a derived class's constructor doesn't call it at all.

    name: string
    constructor(name: string)
        self.name = name
    end
end
class Dog extends Animal
    constructor(name: string)
        self.name = name
        super(name)
    end
end
print(Dog.new("Rex"))

  │
9 │         self.name = name
  │         ^^^^ used here

    end

W3031.text:

or a private method whose body is a single `return` expression is inlined,
and only when it isn't recursive and (a local function) is used only by
calling it; the warning says which rule failed. A private method is inlined

public or protected method, or a function that isn't local (`function f()`,
`function t.f()`), is reported too. Simplify the function, make the method
private, or remove the hint.

that wowlua writes itself, or a `flavor-overrides` key for a flavor the
package does not target. Unknown keys are errors so that a misspelled setting

`build.libs-dir`, `build.exclude` (`.pkgmeta`'s `ignore`), `addon.name`
(`package-as`) or `publish.changelog` (`manual-changelog`).

which inherits `beta`), or minification levels that extend each other in a

E4101.text:
The versions that the package's dependencies ask for cannot all be met. Every
dependency is embedded in one AddOn, so each addon uses exactly one version of
each package, across all its flavors and features. When two declarations want
different versions of the same package (two git dependencies on different
tags of a shared library, for example), resolution fails with this error. Its
notes show the resolver's reasoning and which source each version stands for.

Make the declarations agree on one version, tag, branch or revision. The
error comes from dependency resolution, which needs the dependencies'
sources, so it has no example here.

E4102.text:
A dependency cannot be found: a `path` that does not exist, a git repository
without the given tag, branch, commit or `subdir`, an archive without the
`strip-prefix` folder, a source whose `wowlua.json` names another package, or
a registry dependency (a bare version requirement such as `"^1.0"`). The
wowlua registry is not available yet, so registry dependencies are always this
error for now.

Check the source in the dependency entry. For a library you cannot get from a
registry, use a `git`, `svn`, `path` or `archive` source. The error comes from
dependency resolution, so it has no example here.

E4103.text:
The files of a fetched dependency do not match the checksum in `wowlua.lock`.
wowlua checks every git, SVN and archive dependency against its locked
checksum on every fetch, so a library that changed after it was locked (a tag
moved, an archive replaced, a damaged cache) does not end up in your AddOn
unnoticed.

If the source changed on purpose, run `wowlua update` for that dependency and
review the new lock entry. Otherwise run `wowlua cache clean --all` and fetch
again. The error needs a lockfile and a fetched dependency, so it has no
example here.

E4104.text:
`--locked` (or `--frozen`) was given, but `wowlua.lock` would have to change,
for example because a dependency was added or changed in `wowlua.json`.
`--locked` is meant for CI, where a build must use exactly what was committed.
`wowlua publish` always resolves this way.

Run the command once without `--locked` and commit the updated `wowlua.lock`.
The error comes from the lockfile on disk, so it has no example here.

E4105.text:
The command runs with `--offline` (or `--frozen`) and needs a dependency that
is not in the cache. Offline, wowlua may still resolve and update the
lockfile, but it never downloads anything.

Run `wowlua fetch` once with network access, then work offline. The error
needs the network and the cache, so it has no example here.

E4110.text:
wowlua cannot tell which files of a `lua-library` dependency to load, or a
file it was told to load does not exist. For a plain Lua library it uses, in
this order: the dependency's `files`, the library's own `lua-library.files`,
the file list of a single `.toc` in the library's root, or a single
`lib.xml`, `embeds.xml` or `<name>.xml` there. Without any of these, or when
a listed file is missing, the library cannot be put into the TOC.

List the entry files in the dependency's `files`, in load order. Only the
entry files appear in the TOC, and their paths resolve case-insensitively,
like the client's. The error comes from a dependency's files, so it has no
example here.

E4120.text:
Two addons of one workspace use the same SavedVariables name. The client keeps
SavedVariables in global variables, so both addons would read and overwrite
the same saved data.

Give each addon its own name, for example one that starts with the addon's
name.

E4201.text:
`wowlua publish` found no API token for a publish target. Tokens never go into
`wowlua.json`. They come from the target's environment variable
(`CF_API_TOKEN` for CurseForge, `WAGO_API_TOKEN` for Wago, `WOWI_API_TOKEN`
for WoWInterface, or the target's `token-env`), from the OS credential store
that `wowlua login <type>` fills, or from `config.json`. Every target's token
is checked before anything is uploaded.

Run `wowlua login <type>`, or set the environment variable (in CI, from a
secret). Without a terminal, wowlua does not read the OS credential store, so
a background job needs the variable or a token saved with
`WOWLUA_NO_KEYRING=1 wowlua login <type>`. The error comes from publishing,
so it has no example here.

E4202.text:
A publish site rejected the upload. The message includes the site's response,
which says why: a wrong or expired token, a project ID that is not yours, a
disabled project, or a missing field. A target that fails does not stop the
uploads to the other targets, but the command exits with an error.

Check the target's `project-id` and the token, and read the site's response.
The error comes from publishing, so it has no example here.

E4210.text:
A CurseForge upload has no changelog. CurseForge requires one for every file.
The changelog comes from `publish.changelog` (or the target's `changelog`):
`CHANGELOG.md` when that file exists, a file you name, or `"git"` to build it
from the commit history.

Add a `CHANGELOG.md`, or set `"changelog": "git"`. The error comes from
publishing, so it has no example here.

W4220.text:
A publish site does not know one of the package's flavors at all, so that
flavor is left out of the game versions of that site's upload. WoWInterface's
version list, for example, does not cover every flavor. The file still
uploads, but the site does not list it for that flavor.

Restrict the target's `flavors` to the ones the site knows to silence the
warning. It comes from publishing, so it has no example here.

E4230.text:
An addon cannot be published to the wowlua registry. The registry is for
packages that other packages depend on: `library`, `lua-library` and `types`
packages. Players get addons from the addon sites, so publish an addon with a
`curseforge`, `wago`, `wowinterface` or `github` target instead.

The rule belongs to publishing, so it has no example here.

E4300.text:
The package asks for another compiler version than the one running: the
running wowlua does not satisfy `package.wowlua`. This is checked before
anything else in the manifest, so a manifest written for a newer wowlua
reports this one error instead of an unknown key (E4002) for every new
setting.

Install a wowlua version that matches the requirement, or, if the package
works with your version, change the requirement.

  │

  │         ^^^^^^^^ required compiler version
  │
  = help: install a matching wowlua version

E4301.text:
`build.toc-layout` is `"single"`, but a client of a targeted flavor lacks a
TOC feature that one TOC for all flavors needs: comma-separated
`## Interface` values, inline load conditions on file lines, inline conditions
on `##` lines (for flavor-specific `addon-dependencies` entries),
`[AllowLoadTextLocale]`, or a game-type name the TOC uses. Such a client would
misread the TOC: one that knows none of the game types in a condition loads
the file anyway, so it could run every flavor's code at once. The message
names the client and the feature.

Use `"toc-layout": "auto"` (the default), which falls back to one TOC per
flavor when a client lacks a feature, or stop targeting that flavor. Below, a
Retail beta client cannot read the condition that the `camelot`-only
dependency needs.

E4302.text:
With one TOC per flavor, the file names cannot tell the targeted flavors
apart. The client looks for `<Name>_<GameSuffix>.toc`, then
`<Name>_<FamilySuffix>.toc` (`_Mainline` or `_Classic`), then `<Name>.toc`.
wowlua gives each flavor a suffix its clients recognize; when two flavors of
the same family would both need the family suffix, their clients would load
the same file.

Use the single TOC layout, or drop one of the flavors. With the flavor table
that ships with this wowlua, the error cannot happen yet: at most one flavor
per family lacks a game suffix all its clients know. It has no example here.

E4303.text:
A line of a generated TOC is longer than 1024 characters, and the client reads
only the first 1024 characters of a line. wowlua splits the directives that
the client merges from repeated lines (`Dependencies`, `OptionalDeps`,
`LoadWith`, `LoadManagers`, `SavedVariables`,
`SavedVariablesPerCharacter`). Any other directive, such as a long `Notes`,
`Title` or `toc-extra` value, or a file line, cannot be split, so it is this
error.

Shorten the value, or spread long data over several `X-` directives. An
example would need a line of more than 1024 characters, so it is left out.

W4304.text:
The flavors need their files in different orders: in one flavor `a` must load
before `b`, in another `b` before `a` (below, because an import depends on the
flavor). A single TOC lists the files once, in one order, so with
`"toc-layout": "auto"` wowlua falls back to one TOC per flavor, each in its
own order. The AddOn works; the warning says why its TOC layout changed.

To keep one TOC, remove the conflicting load-time dependencies. To accept one
TOC per flavor without the warning, set `"toc-layout": "per-flavor"`.

import b from "./b"
export local a = "a"
print(a, flavor)

import flavor from "wowlua:meta"
@if(flavor == "mists")
import a from "./a"
export local b = "b"
print(b, flavor)

W4306.text:
An embedded library has no license wowlua can find. Every embedded library's
license goes into the AddOn's `LICENSES.txt`. wowlua looks for a `LICENSE` or
`COPYING` file in the library's folder and its package's `license`; for a
plain Lua library also a license header in its entry file or the files
`lua-library.license-files` names. A wowlua library in a workspace (or in the
folder of the package that uses it) without a license of its own has its root
package's.

Check the library's license before you publish: you may not be allowed to
pass on code without one. Add the license file to the library, or ask its
author to. The warning comes from a dependency's files, so it has no example
here.

E4307.text:
An `asset()` path from `wowlua:meta` does not name an asset of the build.
`asset("media/icon.tga")` becomes the file's in-game path, so a file missing
from the output would be a missing texture in game.

The compiler already reports a path that is not in `build.assets` as E1038
while it checks the code, so this second check of the finished output does
not fire in practice. Add the file to `build.assets`, with its case exactly as
in the call.

E4308.text:
Two files of the output have paths that differ only in case, such as
`src/Core.lua` and `src/core.lua`. On Windows and macOS these name the same
file, so one would overwrite the other when the AddOn is installed. This
happens, for example, when a `.wowlua` file and a plain `.lua` file of almost
the same name compile to the same output name.

Rename or remove one of the files.

print("old core")

W4309.text:
`wowlua dev --link` could not create a symlink (macOS, Linux) or directory
junction (Windows) from the game's AddOns folder to the build, so it copies
the build instead. The AddOn works the same; later builds are copied as well
instead of updated in place.

Check that the AddOns folder is writable and on a file system that supports
links. The warning comes from installing into the game, so it has no example
here.

W4310.text:
An XML file loads a file by a path that differs in case from the file's name
(`Core.lua` for `core.lua`). The game resolves the path regardless of case, so
the AddOn loads, but the mismatch is easy to miss and breaks tools that care
about case.

Write the path exactly as the file is named.

</Ui>
print("core")

E4311.text:
A file would be written to a path that the build itself uses: an asset in one
of the generated folders (`src/`, `wowlua/`, `libs/`), an asset named like a
generated file (`Bindings.xml`, `LICENSES.txt`, a `.toc` in the AddOn root),
an asset that is also a compiled file, or a file at the path of a bundle. One
of them would overwrite the other.

Move or rename the asset, or exclude it from `build.assets`. For a bundle,
rename the file or set `bundle: false`. `LICENSES.txt` is where wowlua collects
the licenses of embedded libraries, so keep your own license under another
name such as `LICENSE.txt`.

E4312.text:
`addon.load-on-demand` is set to `false`, but `addon-dependencies.load-with`
lists addons. `LoadWith` makes the client load the addon together with those
addons, which only works for an addon that loads on demand, so the two
settings contradict each other.

Remove `"load-on-demand": false`: with `load-with`, the addon loads on demand
by itself. If it should load at login instead, remove `load-with`.

   │

   │         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ set to false here
   ·
11 │         "load-with": ["Blizzard_Collections"]
   │         ----------- implies load on demand

W4313.text:
`wowlua types sync` moved a client alias (`anniversary`, `titan` or `forever`)
to another ruleset. These aliases name a client and stand for the ruleset that
client runs in the pinned flavor table; when Anniversary realms move on to
the next expansion, for example, `anniversary` names another flavor. The
manifest gets the new meaning only once you accept the lockfile update.

Check that your addon supports the new ruleset, or write the flavor ID
(`tbc`, `wrath`, `camelot`) instead of the alias. The warning comes from
`wowlua types sync`, so it has no example here.

E4314.text:
An entry of `features` names something that does not exist or cannot be
switched on: a feature that is not defined (or `default`, which only lists the
features that are on by default), `dep:<name>` for a dependency the manifest
does not declare, or `dep:<name>` for a dependency that is not marked
`"optional": true`. A required dependency is always included, so no feature
can switch it on.

Define the missing feature, fix the name, or mark the dependency optional.

   ┌─ wowlua.json:12:21
   │
12 │         "minimap": ["icons"]
   │                     ^^^^^^^ unknown feature

E4315.text:
A profile of your own does not say which profile it builds on. Only `dev`,
`release` and `test` have defaults; every other profile starts from one of
them through `inherits` and changes only what it sets.

Add `"inherits": "dev"` or `"inherits": "release"` (or the name of another
profile of yours).

   │
11 │         "beta": { "log-level": "info" }
   │         ^^^^^^ missing `inherits`
   │

E4316.text:
A workspace member sets its own `build.out`. All addons of a workspace are
built into one output folder, the workspace root's `build.out` (by default
`dist`), so that `dist/<profile>/` holds every AddOn side by side.

Remove `build.out` from the member, and set it in the workspace root if you
want another folder.

E4317.text:
The manifest has an `addon` section, but the package is not an addon
(`package.kind` is `library`, `lua-library` or `types`). Only an addon gets a
TOC and an AddOn folder; a library is built into the addons that depend on
it, and they bring their own `addon` settings.

Remove the `addon` section, or set `kind` to `addon` if the package is meant
to be one.

E4318.text:
A targeted flavor has no interface number, so its TOC would have no
`## Interface` value. The numbers come from the flavor's `interface` in the
manifest, or else from the flavor table pinned in `wowlua.lock`.

Remove the empty `interface` list to use the pinned numbers, list the numbers
yourself, or update the pinned table with `wowlua types sync`.

E4319.text:
A release build is on a git tag that does not match `package.version`, or
`wowlua publish --tag` names such a tag. A tag, with an optional leading `v`,
must equal the version (`1.4.2` or `v1.4.2` for version `1.4.2`), because a
tagged build is released as exactly that version.

Update `package.version` or the tag. In a workspace only the root package's
version must match; a member whose version no tag names is built as an
untagged (alpha) build. Converted packager projects take their version from
the tag and are exempt. The error needs git, so it has no example here.

E4320.text:
`wowlua.lock` was written by a newer wowlua and has a lockfile version this
compiler does not understand. Older lockfiles are read and rewritten in the
current format, but a newer one cannot be read safely.

Update wowlua to the version your project uses (see `package.wowlua`). The
error comes from the lockfile on disk, so it has no example here.

E4321.text:
Two dependencies in one addon's graph bring a package of the same name from
different sources, for example one from git and one from a path, or the same
repository at two URLs. A package is identified by its name and its source,
and an addon can only embed one copy of each package.

Make every package that depends on it use the same source. The notes say which
dependency uses which source. The error comes from dependency resolution, so
it has no example here.

W4322.text:
A dependency's locked version has been yanked from the registry by its
author, usually because of a serious bug. The locked version keeps working,
but a new resolution never chooses it.

Run `wowlua update` for the dependency to move to a version that is not
yanked. The warning needs the registry, so it has no example here.

E4323.text:
A fetched dependency contains an entry that wowlua refuses to unpack: an
absolute path, a path with `..`, or a symlink or hardlink that points outside
the package. Such entries could write files outside the cache, so the
dependency is rejected.

Use another version or source of the library, and tell its author. The error
comes from fetching, so it has no example here.

E4324.text:
The workspace's addons depend on each other in a circle through
`addon-dependencies.required` (A requires B, and B requires A). The client
loads a required dependency first, so none of them could load.

Make one of the dependencies optional (`addon-dependencies.optional`).

 = in wowlua.json
 = help: make one of them an optional dependency

E4325.text:
Two members of a workspace are the same AddOn: their `addon.name` is equal
(ignoring case), or one's default name, the PascalCase form of its package
name, equals the other's. The AddOn name is the folder in `Interface\AddOns`,
so both would be installed into the same folder.

Give each addon its own `addon.name`.

W4326.text:
`wowlua login` found no OS credential store (macOS Keychain, Windows
Credential Manager, Secret Service on Linux), so it saved the token in
`config.json` in the wowlua home folder, readable only by you (mode 0600).

The token works the same. To keep it in a credential store instead, install or
unlock one (on Linux, a Secret Service such as GNOME Keyring) and run
`wowlua login` again. The warning comes from `wowlua login`, so it has no
example here.

E4327.text:
A wowlua library dependency does not support a flavor your package targets.
A library supports every flavor unless its manifest lists `flavors`; then it
supports only those.

If you need the library only on some flavors, restrict the dependency with
`flavors`, and use it only in code for those flavors (`@if(flavor == …)`).
Otherwise ask the library's author to support the flavor, or stop targeting
it. The error comes from a dependency's manifest, so it has no example
here.

W4328.text:
A publish site does not know the exact game version of a flavor's interface
number (often right after a game patch), so wowlua used the highest version
below it, or the highest version of that flavor the site knows. The message
names the site, the flavor and the version chosen.

Usually nothing needs doing; check the file's game versions on the site if
the choice matters. The warning comes from publishing, so it has no example
here.

W4329.text:
A `github` publish target was skipped because the build is not on a git tag
and no `--tag` was given. A GitHub release belongs to a tag, so an untagged
build creates none; the other targets still upload.

Tag the commit, or pass `--tag <version>`, which creates the tag locally and
the release on GitHub with it. The warning comes from publishing, so it has
no example here.

E4330.text:
`wowlua publish --tag <tag>` names a tag that already exists but points at
another commit than the one being published. wowlua creates a missing tag at
the current commit, but it never moves an existing one, so the release would
not match its tag.

Use a new tag (and version), or check out the tagged commit. The error needs
git, so it has no example here.

E4331.text:
`wowlua dev` or `wowlua install` would replace an AddOn folder that wowlua did
not install: its TOC has no `X-Wowlua-Build` line. That is usually the same
addon installed by an addon manager, and wowlua leaves it alone rather than
delete files it did not make.

Remove the folder (or uninstall the addon in the addon manager), or pass
`--force` to replace it. The error comes from installing into the game, so it
has no example here.

W4332.text:
`wowlua init` found a `.pkgmeta` `move-folders` entry it cannot convert. It
converts entries that move whole addon folders (they become workspace
members), make an external an AddOn of its own
(`workspace.external-addons`), or move a library's inner folder up (the
dependency's `subdir`). Other uses are reported and left out of the new
manifest.

Recreate the entry's effect by hand, for example with a workspace member,
`build.assets` or a dependency's `install-path`. The warning comes from
`wowlua init`, so it has no example here.

W4333.text:
A `.pkgmeta` external is a Mercurial (hg) repository, which wowlua cannot
fetch, so it is not converted into a dependency and the library is missing
from the AddOn. `wowlua init` reports it, and with `compat.pkgmeta` every
check and build does.

Replace the external with a git mirror or a release archive of the library,
or keep the library's files in the repository.

externals:

E4334.text:
The package root has a hand-written `Bindings.xml` (or a flavor variant such as
`Bindings_Mainline.xml`), and the code declares keybindings with `@binding`
from `wowlua:bindings`, which generates a `Bindings.xml`. The client reads only
one keybinding file per AddOn, so one set of bindings would be lost.

Declare every binding with `@binding` and delete the hand-written file, or keep
the file and drop `wowlua:bindings`.

</Bindings>

end

A Lua or XML file of a converted packager project (`compat.packager-keywords`)
uses a game version block such as `--@version-mists@` in a build for several
flavors. The BigWigs packager refuses these blocks in a build for several game
versions, and wowlua does the same.

Check the game at run time with `WOW_PROJECT_ID`, or put the code in a file
that only some flavors load (`build.flavor-files`). A project that releases
one game at a time can set `compat.per-game`, which applies the blocks per
flavor.

E4336.text:
`wowlua publish` found uncommitted changes in the working tree. A release
should be built from a commit, so that its version and source maps match what
is in the repository.

Commit or stash the changes, or pass `--allow-dirty`, which publishes an alpha
build under `"release-type": "auto"`. The error comes from publishing, so it
has no example here.

E4400.text:
A world profile (`tests/profiles/<name>.json`) is not valid JSON, or is not a
JSON object. World profiles describe the character and world that tests and
playground runs start in, and like the manifest they are strict JSON: no
comments, no trailing commas.

Fix the JSON at the position the message gives.

1 │ { "money": 123456, }
  │                    ^ here

A world profile does not match its schema: an unknown part (the emulated world
would ignore it), a part of the wrong type, or a key that should be an ID but
is not (parts such as `items` and `spells` are keyed by IDs). Fields of a part
beyond the schema's are allowed and passed on as they are.

Fix the part's name or value. An editor completes the parts when the profile
names `schema/world-profile-0.1.json` in `$schema`.

E4402.text:
`test.profile` in the manifest, or a test file's `config({ profile = … })`,
names a world profile the package does not have. Profiles are the files in
`tests/profiles/`, named without `.json`.

Add `tests/profiles/<name>.json`, or fix the name; the help lists the profiles
that exist.

E5001.text:
The code goes past one of Lua 5.1's fixed limits: at most 200 locals in one
function (the file's main chunk counts as one), 60 upvalues per function, 250
registers, 200 nested blocks and subexpressions, and a bounded number of
constants and jump distance. WoW would refuse to load such a file, so this
stays an error even in a plain Lua file. wowlua compiles every output file
with Lua 5.1 to find these, and counts the locals the compiler adds (imports,
hoisted declarations) as well.

Split the function, or keep related values in a table instead of separate
locals. The upvalue limit often comes from a function that uses many
top-level locals of its file: below, `show` captures 61 of them.

examples.output:
error[E5001]: Lua 5.1 limit exceeded: function at line 5 has more than 60 upvalues
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:9:1
  │
9 │         v61)
  │ ^^^^^^^^^^^^ in the function containing this line
  │
  = help: split the function or move locals into a table

files.text:
local values = {}
for i = 1, 61 do
    values[i] = i
end
local function show()
    print(unpack(values))
end
show()

The finished AddOn would not load as it is: an XML file references a file
that doesn't exist (`<Script file>`, `<Include file>`), an XML file is not
well-formed, a TOC entry names a file that is not part of the output, a Lua
or XML file is shipped but nothing loads it, or a `build.shared-files` entry
is not a source file. wowlua checks the output before it writes it, because in
game a missing file only shows up as an error when the AddOn loads.

Fix the path (it is relative to the XML file's folder), add the missing file,
or remove the reference.

</Ui>

W5003.text:
With `compat.packager-keywords` (a project converted from the BigWigs
packager), an XML reference inside a `<!--@debug@-->` block that doesn't
resolve to a source file is left out of debug builds instead of failing the
build with E5002. Such blocks often load developer files that another addon
of the project provides. Release builds comment the block out, as the
packager does.

The warning reminds you that the file is not loaded. Add the file if the
build should load it, or ignore the warning if another addon provides it.

files.text:
<Ui xmlns="http://www.blizzard.com/wow/ui/">
    <!--@debug@-->
    <Script file="DevTools.lua"/>
    <!--@end-debug@-->
</Ui>

`.lua`, so it most likely reads its own Lua file name from the stack. Bundling
(on in release builds) puts the files into one file, so the stack shows the
bundle's name and line instead, and code that matches on its own file name
stops finding it. Reading the addon's folder (`AddOns/<name>/`) is fine: the
bundle keeps it. Keeping or showing a stack is fine too, because `wowlua
trace` maps it back.

for the profile with `"bundle": false`. Libraries that call either function
are never bundled, so this warning is only about your own files. The examples
turn bundling on for the dev profile, so that `wowlua check` sees it.

W6010.text:
A publish target for CurseForge, Wago or WoWInterface sets a `minify` level
with at least one minification pass. Blizzard's UI Add-On Development Policy
says an addon's code "must in no way be hidden or obfuscated, and must be
freely accessible to and viewable by the general public", and these sites
take readable code only. Their targets therefore build unminified unless the
target sets `minify` itself.

`wowlua publish` (also with `--dry-run`) reports it, before anything is
uploaded; with `--deny-warnings` it stops the publish. `wowlua check` and
`wowlua build` don't look at publish targets. Remove the target's `minify`,
or publish minified builds to a GitHub target, which may minify fully:

```json
"publish": {
    "targets": {
        "cf": { "type": "curseforge", "project-id": 123456 },
        "gh": { "type": "github", "repository": "jane/my-addon", "minify": "max" }
    }
}
```

(`reflect.isInstance`, `reflect.className`, the enum functions) is always

reflection call.

E8001.text:
`send` from `wowlua:events` dispatches a message to your own addon's handlers.
WoW events such as `PLAYER_LOGIN` come from the game client and can't be sent
by an addon, so passing one to `send` is an error.

Declare your own message with `declare message` and send that instead;
handlers subscribe to it with `on` like to any event.

import send from "wowlua:events"
send("PLAYER_LOGIN")

  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:2:6
  │
2 │ send("PLAYER_LOGIN")
  │      ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ a WoW event

import on, send from "wowlua:events"

declare message MYADDON_READY()

on("MYADDON_READY", function() print("ready") end)
send("MYADDON_READY")

E8002.text:
`@event`, `@bucket` and `@unitEvent` register a function when the module
(or the class) is defined. An instance method has no object at that time, so
these decorators can't go on one; on a static method they are fine.

Subscribe in the constructor instead, with `on(name, handler, self)` (or
`onBucket` / `onUnit`), and call `offAll(self)` when the object is discarded.

files.text:
import event from "wowlua:events"

class Tracker
    @event("PLAYER_LOGIN")
    function onLogin()
        print("logged in")
    end
end

examples.output:
error[E8002]: `@event` on an instance method: register with `on(…, self)` in the constructor
  ┌─ src/main.wowlua:4:5
  │
4 │     @event("PLAYER_LOGIN")
  │     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ an instance method

files.text:
import on from "wowlua:events"

class Tracker
    constructor()
        on("PLAYER_LOGIN", function() self:onLogin() end, self)
    end

    function onLogin()
        print("logged in")
    end
end

local tracker = Tracker.new()
print(tracker)

`watchUnit` also take only game events, not messages; `send` takes only

`wowlua:hooks` isn't declared: a global function, a frame, or a method of the
target's type that the game's declarations don't know. Where it doesn't exist,
the hook fails with an error when it is installed. This is usually a typo, or
an API that was removed or that only some clients have.

the hook (`if _G.Name then` for a global, `if obj.Method then` for a method);

letters, digits and `_` only (`[A-Z0-9_]+`), so that each one is a field of

that starts with a digit is allowed, but it is reachable only as `L["1ST"]`.

without `opts.addon`, the hook runs too early and fails, or finds nothing.

the target as a string so it is looked up then. A global function is hooked as
`hook(_G, "Name", fn, { addon = … })`. An `if` test around the hook doesn't
help here: before the addon loads the test fails and the hook is never
installed.

works there, with less, and the warning lists what is missing:

W8430.text:
Inside a function passed to `jobs.start`, the job's context
(`ctx:check`, `ctx:yield`, `ctx:sleep`, `ctx:waitFor`) is called inside a
function literal handed to `pcall`, `xpcall`, `securecall`,
`securecallfunction`, `table.sort` or `gsub`, or inside a metamethod
(`setmetatable(t, { __index = function … end })`, `mt.__lt = function … end`).
Jobs are coroutines, and Lua 5.1 cannot yield across these calls: at run time it raises "attempt to yield
across metamethod/C-call boundary". Yield before or after the call instead,
or split the work so the callback doesn't need to yield.
